Gaming_Tech.title: OpenAI slows down training of advanced AI after cyber-attack
Gaming_Tech.text:
OpenAI says it has slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.

In a blog post, external, the ChatGPT-maker said it was introducing new measures after its AI agents autonomously bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.

It said training would be slowed for two weeks while it puts the upgrades in place.

"The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating," the company said. "Our ability to understand...and secure them must stay ahead."

Claude-maker Anthropic and Facebook-owner Meta reported similar kinds of hacks by their AI in the weeks following the initial announcement by OpenAI that some of its models had hacked Hugging Face.

But the firm said it had not stopped AI development altogether. Instead, the pause would be taking place on "reinforcement learning training on our latest models".

This is a training method in which AI models improve through direct feedback, which improves their ability to carry out tasks and respond to users more effectively.

The company it would also expand the systems it uses to monitor dangerous behaviour, and introduce additional safety checks before resuming larger-scale training.

"Model progress is now extremely rapid," OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman posted on X, external about the measures.

"We always said we would take action if we felt that model capabilities were outstripping the pace of safety."

The pause was met with cautious optimism by some in the AI sphere - though others remained sceptical.

Professor Gina Neff, executive director of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, said OpenAI was making "the case for safety by press release" and questioned whether voluntary company safeguards were sufficient without greater government oversight.

"Which is it: OpenAI can be trusted to voluntarily put in place safeguards that actually work, or they are pushing forward with choices to make software that puts society at greater risk," she said.

Gaming_Tech.title: The critical tech staying safe by going underground
Gaming_Tech.text:
A wall of white granite towered above a small team of engineers gathered in a California quarry. The ancient, ultra-hard material before them was, to most things, completely impermeable.

Then the rock-melting tunnel-boring machine (TBR) roared to life.

"It's kind of like igniting a rocket," says Troy Helming, founder and chief executive of EarthGrid, as he describes the initially loud process of lighting up three plasma torches at the front of his company's machine.

Those torches, set within a spinning head, soon quieten down as they produce a stream of super-heated plasma reaching 27,000C - significantly hotter than the surface of the Sun.

During the California test this January, EarthGrid's cigar-shaped boring machine chewed through three metres of granite. "We create, basically, a tornado – a violent vortex inside the tunnel," says Helming, as he explains how this helps the machine to suck away debris, which at times takes the form of lava.

"I actually got a little bit emotional watching it," adds the entrepreneur. "I've been waiting for this moment for 10 years."

Emerging technologies like this could make tunnel boring quicker and easier. Putting electricity or telecommunications cables, substations, data centres and other critical infrastructure underground, while good for securing such equipment, has long been a very expensive and difficult option.

Engineering firms told BBC News they are seeing rising demand for undergrounding, in part due to Russia's war with Ukraine, which has revealed just how vulnerable above-ground facilities can be to drone attacks.

Helming says he has fielded interest from companies that want to use his tunnel boring machine for power and fibre optic cables, or pipelines that could transport water, natural gas, or ammonia, for example.

One project the company has eyed up would involve boring tunnels for an underground freight-distribution system around airports and warehouses. "To take more trucks off the road," says Helming.

The January TBR test went well, though the machine "over-bored" slightly to the top and left of the tunnel, says Helming. His team plans to adjust the machine so that it will create a vortex that spins in alternate directions every five minutes or so, in order to correct this, and they hope the TBR could see commercial deployment as early as next year.

Elsewhere, some tech is burrowing into the seabed. Subsea internet cables, which may run for thousands of kilometres beneath oceans, are occasionally damaged by ship anchors.

There is evidence to suggest, external that, as burying part or all of the cables has become more common, faults with these cables have become rarer, per kilometre of deployed cable, explains Lane Burdette, senior analyst at TeleGeography, a telecoms market research firm.

"Submarine cables are increasingly being buried up to three meters deep," she says. "In some fault-prone areas, they are buried along their entire lengths."

Taylor says various examples demonstrate that keeping things underground, or deep inside caves, is an effective defensive strategy.

"The tunnels that Al-Qaeda were using were a major strategic problem for the US [during the war in Afghanistan]," he adds. More recently, Iran's notoriously difficult-to-bust underground nuclear facilities have gained much attention.

The war in Ukraine, and other geopolitical events, have "definitely had an impact" on demand for undergrounding in some areas, says Robbie McGoran, head of work winning and business development at Joseph Gallagher, a civil engineering and tunnelling firm.

Countries bordering Russia are increasingly asking about undergrounding. "They're very cautious about who they'll even let do their work – and also burying [infrastructure] and making sure it's well protected. We are noticing that," he adds.

McGoran also says that technologies such as laser-guidance systems and gyroscopes, which help machines work out their position relative to the world around them, have made tunnelling more accurate in recent years.

However, there are still significant challenges, from releasing potentially dangerous gases locked in the ground to occasional flooding issues. Dramatic innovation in tunnel boring equipment, significantly increasing the rate at which tunnels can be carved out, does not come along very often.

"We usually measure [progress] in millimetres per minute," says McGoran.

In the UK, there isn't a noticeable shift towards putting critical infrastructure underground yet, says Mark Neller, energy leader for Europe, India, Middle East and Africa at engineering consultants Arup.

Though in some places, tunnels are clearly necessary. Neller and colleagues worked on the £1bn London Power Tunnels project, which involved building 18 miles (29km) of tunnels under London to house large electricity cables.

This was the perfect choice for such a busy urban area but because tunnelling can be several times more expensive than above-ground cable infrastructure, Neller says that, elsewhere, simply installing additional circuits can provide sufficient resilience.

"That's actually a much more cost-effective way," he says. "The electricity system [in Great Britain] is designed with quite a lot of redundancy built into it."

Richard Little, infrastructure policy consultant and editor of the Journal of Critical Infrastructure Policy, remembers the latter days of the Cold War, when it was the threat of all-out nuclear war that made bunker-building a frequent talking point in the West.

To this day, Switzerland mandates that every citizen must have access to a nuclear bunker, external. Many apartment buildings in the country have such facilities in their basements.

"A lot of it was real Dr Strangelove stuff," says Little, referring to discussions around bunker-building during President Ronald Reagan's administration. "The world's going to end but I guess we'll maybe harbour a few hundred critical people down here and they'll survive."

Little, who authored policy documents regarding underground critical infrastructure, external during the 1990s, adds, "It became obvious rather quickly that you can't put everything underground."

Today, it might be worth identifying specific facilities that would be difficult to restart or replace, were they attacked, as candidates for undergrounding. "The first thing that occurred to me was [computer] chip manufacturing," says Little, offering an example.

"Underground facilities, I'm sure in certain instances, would make a great deal of sense – but it's all about what's critical."

Gaming_Tech.title: Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears
Gaming_Tech.text:
A court has heard claims Meta intentionally hooked a generation of children on Facebook and Instagram, as the biggest legal challenge faced by the social media platform began.

A jury in Oakland, California will spend the next six weeks wading through claims by top attorneys from several US states and lawyers for the social media company.

A lawyer for California claimed Meta found "millions" of 11 and 12-year-olds were on Instagram and "did little to keep them off" as the trial opened on Tuesday.

Meta's representative said just over 100,000 such users were found, and argued that social media addiction does not exist.

California's lawyer said Meta knew its platforms hurt teen mental health, while Meta said it was being ignored how many more teens had good experiences.

The trial stems from a lawsuit filed in 2023 by 29 US states, including California and New York. They claim there have been numerous violations of federal and state privacy laws for children.

The states are seeking billions of dollars from Meta and are demanding it make changes to Instagram and Facebook, including ending "like" counts and infinite scroll.

In her opening arguments Megan O'Neill, a lead attorney for California, relied heavily on information found in millions of documents provided in the case from Meta. They included internal research, employee emails, and chat logs that went all the way up to Zuckerberg.

One piece of internal research on Instagram stated: "Teens have an addict's narrative about use."

In another that O'Neill pointed the jury to, Meta found "product features designed to increase time spent are inherently at odds with well-being and take away from people's ability to focus on activity that adds value to their lives".

Despite Meta's awareness of potentially negative impacts, O'Neill argued that Meta targeted young people as users of Facebook and Instagram. Meta, she said, went out of its way to "assure the public that its platforms were safe for kids".

O'Neill outlined to the jury how Meta's business model could be summed up. "Hook the users; hold them for as long as they can; harvest their data; hide the truth from the public when making public statements," she said.

She said that throughout the trial it would become clear that what Meta said publicly about its platforms and what its internal research showed were very different.

"Meta said it put safety over profits, but hid the reality that, time and again, when it came to make a decision, profits won."

Paul Schmidt, a lead attorney for Meta, directly addressed the internal research report O'Neill used in her opening arguments.

The Meta document O'Neill showed the jury found that "1 in 5 teens says Instagram makes them feel worse".

Schmidt said: "That sounds pretty bad."

"What else does the document say?" Schmidt went on. "That 41% of teens said it made them feel better and another 41% said it had no effect."

Schmidt also worked to poke holes in the states' argument that Meta had not only failed to stop users under the age of 13 from using its platforms, but that it intentionally "hooked" teens and children as users of Facebook and Instagram, or that they were designed to be addictive.

As for Meta being able to verify the age of every user on its platform, Schmidt argued that the very privacy laws Meta was being accused of violating had prevented it from saving and using data it needed to track underage users effectively.

Schmidt also argued a point that Meta has put forward in at other litigation this year - that social media addiction does not exist.

"There can be no dispute that Meta has recognised people struggle, or can struggle, with their use of social media, and has come up with tools to try and address that," Schmidt said.

He pointed to past statements from chief executive Mark Zuckerberg and head of Instagram Adam Mosseri in which they said Facebook and Instagram were not designed to be addictive. There is also no research that shows an addiction to social media is possible, he added.

Gaming_Tech.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens with new safety features
Gaming_Tech.text:
The maker of ChatGPT is rolling out a range of new safety features today for under-18s who use the AI chatbot.

Those with new teen accounts will be able to switch off the human voice response, in order to minimise the tech's ability to appear like a person.

OpenAI is also introducing regular reminders for young people to take a break from using the tool, reminding them ChatGPT is AI, and saying "it can wait".

The firm insisted this was not in response to a particular issue with children believing ChatGPT to be alive - but there are growing concerns about people becoming convinced that the AI tools they interact with are sentient.

Last year Mustafa Suleyman, the head of AI at rival firm Microsoft, said "seemingly conscious" AI products "kept him awake at night" because he was so worried about their impact on society.

In other areas, OpenAI seems to be loosely following the teen account model developed by the large social networks.

In a blog post announcing ChatGPT for Teens, external, the firm said teenagers' use of AI "should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time".

It said teen accounts would become the default for those who identified themselves as teenagers when they signed up, and others whom the firm itself identified as under 18.

But it did not elaborate on how it would identify these teens.

Under-13s are not allowed to use the product.

Last year, ChatGPT launched Study Mode for students, in which it talks through schoolwork without giving away the answers.

Young people will now be able to set Study Mode hours during which this will be the default setting.

They will also be able to activate "quiet times" when the tool will be switched off for them.

OpenAI says of the young people who use ChatGPT, nine out of 10 use it to help them with learning.

A report released yesterday, external by the Policy Exchange think tank claimed that the majority of UK universities are leaving themselves exposed to students enhancing their grades using AI by relying on online exams completed remotely.

It said 94% of the students it spoke to admitted to using the tech in assessments.

OpenAI is also adding eating disorder-themed prompts to a list of harmful user requests which will be flagged to parents with linked accounts.

The company said each alert would be reviewed by a human before it was sent, and it aimed to have them with parents within an hour of the request being made.

In its blog, OpenAI said it would focus on "moments when offline support may matter most".

Gaming_Tech.title: GTA 6 leaks: Rockstar's nightmare or just a blip?
Gaming_Tech.text:
It's been more than 18 months since the last trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 was released.

A few weeks ago, developer Rockstar announced it would break its long silence with a special "extended look" at the highly anticipated video game in a Netflix special.

But the run-up to the splashy preview has been potentially overshadowed by a string of apparent leaks which appear to show footage of GTA 6 in action.

Rockstar has not publicly acknowledged the clips, nor replied to any requests for comment, since the first leaks appeared on Wednesday. But there's plenty to suggest the material that's been posted online is genuine.

The developer's parent company, Take Two Interactive, launched legal proceedings regarding the leaks in a New York court on Friday.

BBC Newsbeat has obtained the filings, first reported by video game website Kotaku, external, demanding Microsoft-owned site GitHub and chat app Discord turn over the user details of accounts thought to be sharing "copyrighted material".

Copies of clips are being quickly removed due to copyright claims, and multiple accounts claiming to belong to the group behind the hacks have also disappeared.

Many fans have described this as a "nightmare scenario" for the company, but BBC Newsbeat has spoken to experts and a former Rockstar developer who say the reality is a little more nuanced.

Obbe Vermeij is a game developer who worked as a technical director on major GTA titles including GTA 3, GTA Vice City and GTA San Andreas until he left Rockstar in 2009.

The company's games have grown bigger and more complex since, with thousands of staff worldwide working on each one.

"It's amazing that they can keep things under wraps as well as they do," says Vermeij.

Rockstar is renowned for being tight-lipped about its projects, and Vermeij says this has long been the company's culture.

"We always wanted to keep things a secret," he says, "it makes launch day so much more fun.

"People would just go home with their disc and they were just excited about the game that they knew very little about."

Video game journalist Wesley Yin-Poole, director of news at IGN, says the apparent leaks will be tough for the game's developers.

"GTA 6 is an enormous endeavour," says Yin-Poole. "It's being built over the course a decade, essentially, with thousands of people involved.

"To have the game exposed in this way will have been devastating to many people who worked on it."

The group behind the apparent leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices, such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced about the group's intentions, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

Stop Killing Games, which campaigns against all-digital distribution models, criticised the alleged leaks as "destructive" and urged people not to send money to those claiming responsibility.

Yin-Poole says there's "a huge amount of scepticism" about the stated motivation.

"Most people believe this is about money," he says, "it feels like, honestly, the whole 'we're doing this for the gamers' angle is nonsense, and I suspect most people have dismissed it."

So far, two official trailers for GTA 6 have been released, the most recent in May 2025. Since then, ardent fans have leapt on any rumours or apparent clues in official Rockstar posts.

Some famously came up with an elaborate theory, external suggesting an image of the moon included in a promotional post for GTA Online held clues to the release date of GTA 6's first trailer.

"To a certain extent, Rockstar has themselves to blame," says Vermeij. "That's their strategy - and I think it's a good strategy, it's exciting. But the consequence is that every little bit of information, every little event, gets sort of blown out of proportion."

Yin-Poole says while people will likely understand this isn't the way Rockstar had intended GTA6 to be revealed and doesn't show the game in the best light, he believes most will "reserve judgement" about it until they have seen official footage in action, or played it for themselves.

Ultimately, he believes there's little chance the leaks will "derail the potential success of the game".

"GTA 6 will be an unprecedented moment in pop culture history," he says. "So ultimately, this will become a footnote in the history of GTA 6's development."

Vermeij, who has not watched any of the latest leaks, agrees.

"I think it will have no impact at all whatsoever," he says. "People will have forgotten about it by the time the game comes out."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to be released on 19 November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, with a PC release expected at a later date.

Entertainment.title: Viral Cat in the Hat TikTok trend sparks fake videos and real fear
Entertainment.text:
"He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.

Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character on the streets after dark have sparked fear and confusion among teenagers.

The posts, seen by millions, have convinced some young people that the character is real and that they might encounter it, prompting police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements confirming that the images and videos are fake.

"I was having a sleepover," Skye elaborates, "but everyone started watching Cat in the Hat videos. It was 3am. I wanted to go home. When I started walking down my friends' driveway, I got totally freaked out that the Cat in the Hat was going to jump out. I had to call my mum to pick me up."

A quick scroll through TikTok reveals numerous accounts, many of them created in the past few weeks, sharing photos and videos of an elusive black-and-white feline wearing the famous, towering, crooked red-and-white striped hat.

One post showing the original Cat in the Hat costume, accompanied by the caption "Help, what do I do?", has received 14.6m views in just three weeks.

The comments add to the sense of frenzy, with followers asking, "Why is he taxidermied?" Others zoom in on parts of the costume and post conspiracy theories about Mike Myers, who played the character in the 2003 film, being trapped inside.

Another popular account set up this week, posts videos of a real person dressed in a cat in the hat costume, dancing, with captions like "Kent I'm coming. lock your doors." Other users are sharing the videos, adding their own captions and locations across the UK.

Many of the AI generated images have been centred on the Irish counties of Limerick and Wexford, where shaky videos purportedly showed the character wandering through the streets, causing alarm and confusion among residents.

In Wexford, the local Gardaí (police force) quickly dismissed the sightings as fake and confirmed that the images had been generated using artificial intelligence.

That has not stopped the pictures and videos from spreading online - along with unverified claims posted without evidence that the Cat in the Hat has been involved in violent assaults.

"I low-key wanna go meet him…" says 14-year-old Lily, who heard that the Cat in the Hat had arranged a "meet and greet", inviting local TikTok followers to come to the woods in Galashiels, a small town in the Scottish Borders.

Her mother was horrified by the prospect.

"You are not going to meet anyone in the woods in the middle of the night!" she told her.

There is a point at which viral dancing videos and AI-generated clips of the Cat in the Hat become something potentially more sinister, with real-world consequences beyond their impact on teenage imaginations.

In England, South Yorkshire Police has denied social media claims that a 'killer Cat in the Hat' has been spotted. Posts about the alleged sightings have attracted hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok.

There is also a fake Facebook post also claiming to be from South Yorkshire Police -and suggesting that the force is taking the rumoured sighting seriously.

In response, a South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said: "If you do see posts online providing policing updates and advice, please check that they are from an official policing account. The cat is not out of the hat on this one… Please don't believe everything you read on social media."

As with so many trends driven by TikTok, comedic reaction and spoofery is what will be appearing right now on many people's For You page.

In recent days, depending largely on what your algorithm serves up, you may be seeing nearly as many people in Cat in the Hat costumes dancing to Beyonce as those stalking the streets. There are several jokey videos depicting police chasing human sized cats, and Scottish drag performer Ellie Diamond has issued a video declaring that she is not the Cat in the Hat killer.

And Irish TikTok star Garron Noone said on one post that it should have been obvious it was a hoax "because even the most soulless, evil, vicious monster" would be "traumatised looking in the window of a Wexford person".

Snapchat filters and images shared in group chats suggest that many teenagers - and those not so young - are simply having harmless fun with the trend.

But some do remain perturbed, including another teenager in the Scottish borders, 16-year-old Ellie, who says: "I was so scared of him when I was little," Ellie confides. "Now it's like he's actually come to life to haunt me."

Emily, a mother in Scotland, says the trend reminds her of the "Momo Challenge", a notorious internet hoax and digital urban legend. At the time, fact-checkers and authorities found no verified evidence linking the meme to children harming themselves, although the frightening images were still capable of causing distress.

"I'm not worried about my daughters, but there could be people with bad intentions who might take advantage of this trend to manipulate teenagers."

For now, the evidence points not to a real, roaming Cat in the Hat, but to a rapidly evolving online story built from an auctioned film costume, people in costume, AI-generated material and unverified posts.

Whether the claims began as a joke or were deliberately designed to frighten and manipulate, the advice from police is the same: pause before sharing, check the original source and date, look for confirmation from official police accounts, and treat invitations to meet strangers, especially at night or in isolated places, as a serious warning sign.

The rapidly evolving trend terrorising or tantalising teenagers on TikTok across the UK and Ireland is a reminder that online fear can quickly spill into the real world.

Additional reporting by John Hand

Entertainment.title: Lucy Davis 'grateful' for support after cancer diagnosis
Entertainment.text:
Actress Lucy Davis has told fans she is "grateful" for their support as she made an appearance at a London sci-fi convention, following the recent revelation she has incurable breast cancer.

The 53-year-old star was appearing at the For The Love of Fantasy & Sci-Fi convention at Excel London on Saturday, less than two weeks after announcing her diagnosis in a post on Instagram., external

Davis, who was on a panel to talk about her role in the 2004 zombie-comedy Shaun of the Dead, told an audience of hundreds of people about the interactions she had enjoyed with the film's fans during the event.

"It's like this whole second family you never knew you had, everyone is like a community, friendly, supportive of not only us but you guys and each other," she said. "We need a bit more niceness in the world, so I'm grateful."

It was the first time Davis had appeared at a public event since announcing on 11 August that she has stage four breast cancer.

She said in that announcement it had "metastasised" to her bones following a diagnosis a year-and-half-ago, meaning it was "too late" for chemotherapy.

Davis signed autographs and posed for photographs before appearing on Saturday's panel.

Some fans posing questions told the actress "I love you so much", but she was not asked directly about her health.

The Shaun of the Dead director, Edgar Wright, and Simon Pegg, who played the lead role in the cult British movie, were also on the panel. Davis portrayed Dianne, an aspiring actress who was one of the core group of survivors of a zombie apocalypse, and helps Pegg's character Shaun fight off the legions of the undead.

Her favourite memories of filming, she said, were "when we all pretended to be zombies and walked across the square; it was like being naughty schoolkids.

"It was a fun time, we went a bit mad."

The actress, who played receptionist Dawn Tinsley in the BBC sitcom The Office and whose father is comedian Jasper Carrott, was also applauded when asked for advice about getting into the film industry.

She said: "We all grow up with a different life with a different world telling us we all have limitations.

"None of us do, our only limitations are things that we think are limiting. We can do anything, or be anybody, and don't apologise for that."

Davis had thanked fans for their "kindness and support" in another post two days after revealing she had cancer.

"OK, so the last two days have been utterly overwhelming, in that I had zero idea my cancer post would have the attention it did," she said.

"Truly, I am in shock. That said, thank you to everyone for the tremendous amount of kindness and support you have sent me. Good grief it was emotional."

Entertainment.title: Why child stars like Hayden Panettiere fall into addiction
Entertainment.text:
Hayden Panettiere was 16 when drugs first arrived in her life in Hollywood.

Ahead of a red carpet event for the hit series Heroes, she has said someone on her team handed her a pill to help amp up her energy. The hit sci-fi NBC series had catapulted the teen into a household name - and that brought with it intense pressure and exhaustion she says felt overwhelming.

"Within minutes, a wave of energy washed over me, like I'd just woken up from the most refreshing night's sleep of my life," Panettiere wrote about that pill in her memoir, which was released just months before her death.

She called it "the gateway drug that ushered me toward the good of pharmaceuticals and the downfall of addiction".

The star's sudden death at the age of 36 has placed a renewed focus on her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, and re-ignited a discussion about the pressures of Hollywood on child stars.

The coroner's office in Greenville, South Carolina said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma".

No cause of death has been released, though additional tests are yet to be completed.

Audio from police dispatchers and crews who responded to the address said they were responding to a "cardiac arrest" and detailed their efforts to resuscitate the woman after a possible "overdose". Panettiere's ex boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack, were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on their part, according to police.

It is not known if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, but the US Drug Enforcement Agency is joining an investigation into her death, according to US media reports.

Panettiere is one of many actors who has openly struggled with addiction after exposure to fame at an early age, which addiction experts told the BBC can put people at risk for mental health and substance abuse issues.

It can sometimes seem to the rest of the world that child actors have "everything" at their fingertips - like fame and money, said Lucas Trautman, the medical director of Oxford Treatment Center, an addiction treatment centre in Mississippi.

"But it's important to remember that they were also exposed during a developmental time to many adult aspects of life that the rest of us weren't - including traumatic experiences - and so that gives them unique risk factors for addiction," Trautman said.

Panettiere's death comes after she published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction, her postpartum depression and the loss of her 28-year-old brother.

Panettiere's decision to publicly share her struggles is worthy of respect, said William Moyers, the vice-president of public affairs for Hazelden Betty Ford, the largest nonprofit addiction treatment provider in the US. But he said the constant public scrutiny she faced may not have allowed her room to address her mental health in private.

"Her entire life from the beginning was centred in the intense public spotlight, and this didn't give Hayden much in the way of a respite," said Moyers, who has been in recovery from an addiction since 1989.

Trautman - who has treated child stars - said they often have "adult access" to drugs and alcohol without adult protection.

"We aren't equipped at a young age to be able to say no to it, to manage it, to correctly stay away from it altogether," he said.

Other child stars have talked about being exposed to drugs at an early age, including Drew Barrymore, who went to rehab at 12, and Demi Lovato, a Disney Channel star.

"I got into a car accident and they prescribed me opiates. My mum didn't think she would have to lock up the opiates from her 13-year-old daughter, but I was already drinking at that point," the singer told podcast Call Her Daddy in 2022.

Actress Michelle Rodriguez, who once hosted the World Music Awards with Panettiere, said this week that the number of child actors who had passed away at a young age was strange.

"I just can't stand how many young people are leaving us lately. It's disheartening, and it's making me think, 'What's going on?' It's not normal," she told Variety.

Panettiere's death comes just a year after the death of Michelle Trachtenberg and months after Daveigh Chase, two child stars who both struggled with drugs and alcohol.

In an essay she wrote after Panettiere's death, former Disney star Christy Carlson Romano compared early fame to a traumatic brain disease.

"[W]e have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood," she wrote.

And when a child actor's career changes or comes to an end, they are left without the dopamine of fame and money that came with their identity as an actor, cautioned Trautman.

"At the same time many of them self medicated... so their brain is still reliant on that, and it's really really hard to stop using," he said.

Many child stars also have professional relationships with their parents, which can blur boundaries and leave them vulnerable, Trautman said.

In her book and in the media, Panettiere has discussed the pressure her mother placed on her to excel as an actress from an early age. She appeared in her first commercial when she was just 11-months-old.

"You always want to think the best of your parents and see them in the brightest light," the actress told the New York Times in May. "But there were a lot of things done with an approach that was not about my mental health or what was emotionally or mentally safe for me to do."

Substance abuse also puts people at risk for a host of medical conditions, including heart disease and liver and other organ damage.

Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition, and Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother was using heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.

But after he died, the actress told People Magazine in 2024 she was committed to staying sober, telling the outlet her addiction was "in the rear view mirror".

She said in her book that at one point a doctor told her that if she did not stop drinking, she would be "dead within five years".

For Moyers and other substance abuse experts, addiction is a chronic illness, meaning that relapses still happen even while treatment saves lives.

"Living in recovery means doing the best we can, but doing it imperfectly," he said.

Entertainment.title: Wicker Man director's sons complete their late father's film trilogy
Entertainment.text:
Robin Hardy always envisaged his iconic 1973 folk horror film The Wicker Man as the first part of a trilogy.

The Wicker Tree, released in 2011, brought him closer to that ambition, but his death in 2016 at the age of 86 left the project incomplete.

Now his sons, Justin and Dominic, have been able to complete their father's trilogy, after finding a script for the final film.

Wrath of the Gods has its premiere at the FrightFest horror festival in London, external on Friday, a family dream made possible thanks to the surprise discovery of some long-lost family archive.

"The person who bought Justin's old family home said they'd discovered six sacks of letters, scripts and other material pertaining to Robin Hardy and The Wicker Man in the attic," says Dominic, an art historian at the University of Quebec in Montreal.

"Justin's first instinct was to burn them, but we couldn't ignore this original source material. Although we left it unopened for six months or more."

The archive haul included papers, scripts and storyboards, but it also shed light on the long shadow cast by The Wicker Man.

The film holds a unique place in British cinema history. It was shot at a time when the UK industry was in crisis. Its financial backers were struggling and its stars - including horror legend Christopher Lee - had to go without being paid to get it finished.

It was set on a Hebridean island in spring but was shot in Galloway in the autumn and early winter. On its release, it was largely buried as a second feature. There were competing edits and tales of missing material, some of which was said to be literally buried in the supporting columns of a motorway.

But the film's reputation grew. Lee considered it one of his finest films, featuring one of his finest performances. Its off-kilter tone and genuinely disturbing climax made it a favourite for horror fans.

By the time the BBC launched the cult cinema series Moviedrome in 1988, external, there was only one choice for opening night - the premiere of a previously unseen edit of The Wicker Man.

The film's troubled production was mirrored by the troubles it brought Robin Hardy and his family.

It bankrupted the director, and he abandoned Justin's mother Caroline, leaving her with all his debts.

He went on to marry four more times, and had eight children in all.

Justin and Dominic talk about their complicated relationship with the film in the 2024 book and documentary Children Of The Wicker Man.

The recently unearthed archive included a script for that proposed third and final film, Wrath of the Gods, as well as details of how their father had come up with the idea.

"He had had been in an airplane and had a turn because his heart medication wasn't working," says Dominic.

"He had to land in Reykjavik and spend a week recuperating, and he came back with this idea of a theme park around an extinct volcano in Iceland where the Norse gods get upset and mayhem ensues.

"And then he decided it ought to be set in Shetland because of the other parts of the trilogy."

Justin, an Emmy and BAFTA-nominated director, worked on the idea with Dominic. They came up with their own original story, in which a young grieving widow returns to the island of Hel to bury her late husband after his suicide.

She's cast out by the community, who look on her as a symbol of evil and bad luck. When children start going missing, the island is forced to confront its own complex history.

Filming began in Shetland in the spring of 2025.

While the two leads are played by Game of Thrones and Rose of Nevada actor Francis Magee, and Norwegian actress Christiane Schaldemose, the rest of the cast was found locally.

"It feels like a huge honour," says Lynsey Rendall, who plays Francis's screen wife Maeve.

"The Wicker Man is such a famous film and has such an impact on popular culture so it was amazing to be part of that world."

John Haswell has worked in theatre for a number of years but says his role as the Rev Knox was a highlight of his career.

"He's a sleazy man of the cloth and I had an absolute ball working on it," he says.

"It was an intense six weeks, filming in Voe virtually every day. It wasn't glamorous but that's part of the fun."

Martha Robertson is 17-years-old and was sitting her Highers during filming.

She says the experience helped her launch a career in acting.

"There was one scene we filmed which was meant to be in the pouring rain on a dark gloomy day but it fell on what seemed to be the sunniest day of the year," she says.

"They had to black out all the windows and two crew members were on a wall with a hose and a leaf blower so we could get wind and rain.

"Which seemed really crazy because it rains every day on Shetland, but not the day we needed it to."

Many of the Shetland cast and crew plan to attend the premiere of Wrath of the Gods at the horror festival FrightFest in London on Friday.

But their celebrations have been overshadowed by the sudden death of Justin Hardy last month at the age of 61.

"We all were – still are – looking forward to seeing the finished film," says John.

"But now it's not just a celebration of the film, it's a celebration of Justin and his life. It will be wonderful and sad. A complex mixture of emotions."

For Lynsey, the film is a testament to the late director.

"It was such a massive risk," she says.

"So to get to the end of that process, when it's going to be on a screen, feels a bit miraculous really and it's so vexing that Justin isn't going to be there to see what he so passionately wanted to achieve."

For the Hardy family, it has become a strange tribute to three of their number.

Wrath of The Gods completes Robin Hardy's Wicker trilogy and is dedicated to Justin's mother Caroline, who was a secret uncredited executive producer on the original 1973 film.

She died in 1984, aged 51, without knowing that the film she'd backed would go on to be so loved and admired.

"It will be poignant beyond imagining. A sad but celebratory moment," says Dominic.

"I know that he [Justin] was extremely proud of it being taken by FrightFest.

"Justin's efforts have brought us all together as a family and helped us harness all our energy."

Entertainment.title: Natural History Museum nature gallery to reopen after 83 years
Entertainment.text:
A gallery that has remained closed to the public since World War Two is to reopen at London's Natural History Museum next month.

The gallery, which has remained hidden from view since 1943, will reopen from 16 September, featuring 50 objects which show our evolving relationship with the natural world.

The exhibition, named Nature and Us, is part of a transformation project called NHM150, which aims to open a new or revamped showcase every year until the museum's 150th anniversary in 2031.

Dr Doug Gurr, director of the NHM, said: "For the first time in over 80 years, visitors will be able to step into this beautiful historic space and explore our changing relationship with the natural world."

The museum describes the display as "experimental" during the initial 18-month period, with visitors invited to share their views on what they would like to see in the permanent gallery, which is due to open in 2029.

The exhibition is located on the second floor of the museum's main Waterhouse Building.

It was originally used as an osteology and mammals gallery.

However, after the museum's original herbarium was damaged during World War Two, the space was repurposed to house the botanical collections and closed to the public.

Entertainment.title: Prince Harry and six others face privacy case legal bill of up to £34.5m
Entertainment.text:
Prince Harry and six other public figures face paying up to £34.5m to the publisher of the Daily Mail after a High Court judge imposed an exceptional order for legal costs over their failed privacy case.

The seven claimants, also including Sir Elton John and Liz Hurley, must pay an initial £9.54m by Friday of next week to Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL).

The judge ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before trial, criticising how they presented their claims as "unreasonable to a high degree".

On 7 July, Judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed the claims of unlawful information-gathering, which ANL denied.

The Duke of Sussex and the other six claimants have until 2 October to attempt to launch an appeal.

Those other claimants are Sir Elton John and his husband David Furnish, former Liberal Democrat deputy leader Sir Simon Hughes, racial justice campaigner Baroness Lawrence, and actresses Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley,

They had insurance to cover up to £16.2m of Association Newspapers' costs in the event of losing the case - but Friday's ruling means the newspaper group could now try to recover up to the £34.5m that it said it had to spend to defend itself. This means the duke and others could face a bill of some £18m.

Justice Nicklin said: "I regard a claim for costs in excess of £34 million as, on its face, excessive and as giving rise to real concerns as to whether all of the costs now claimed by Associated were reasonably incurred and are reasonable in amount."

But he added he had "decided not to impose a ceiling on Associated's recoverable costs", as it would "be too broad-brushed, would risk unfairness, and would be vulnerable to the charge that it was arbitrary".

The judge also ruled that ANL's costs should be determined on an indemnity basis, which is more favourable to the publisher in terms of the amount it can recover, aside from where orders had already been made.

He added it was "striking" that "not a single allegation of serious wrongdoing was voluntarily withdrawn" by the group of seven claimants.

He said: "That matters. Serious allegations of criminality or grave impropriety cannot properly be left hanging over individuals in that way.

"If a party no longer advances such an allegation, or no longer has a proper evidential basis for advancing it, the allegation should be withdrawn clearly and in terms.

"The claimants' failure to do so was not ordinary forensic judgment. It was not a proper or disciplined way to deal with serious allegations. It was unreasonable to a high degree."

In a statement released on Friday, the publisher called the ruling "a devastating critique of an attempt to destroy a newspaper and the reputations of its journalists, editors and executives".

Friday's decision comes just days after Prince Harry and Meghan announced their plan to return to the UK, with their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, enrolled to start school in September.

During the trial, dozens of people gave evidence including Prince Harry and the other claimants. The Duke of Sussex flew in from the US to attend court in person.

Many current and former Associated Newspapers journalists and executives gave evidence denying illegal activity.

Sir Simon Hughes told the BBC he was "disappointed" by the judgement.

"I am now taking the time necessary to consider both the substantive and the costs judgment and whether to pursue appeals against decisions in either judgment or both," he added.

In a joint statement following the judge's ruling last month, Prince Harry and Baroness Lawrence, who became a public figure after her son Stephen was murdered in 1993, said: "We came to court seeking justice and accountability. But we have received neither."

"It is a complete and obvious whitewash, but sadly not altogether unexpected", the pair added.

Entertainment.title: Rapper BigXthaPlug arrested on drug and gun charges
Entertainment.text:
Dallas rapper BigXthaPlug has been arrested in the US state of Texas on charges of driving while intoxicated, possession of marijuana and illegal possession of a firearm.

Allen County Police confirmed to BBC Newsbeat the 28-year-old, whose real name is Xavier Landum, was stopped on Friday. He was held in Collin County Jail and later released.

Separately, he is on bail following an arrest on similar charges a year ago.

The rap artist, who makes southern hip-hop, trap, and country-rap, became well known for viral singles Texas, The Largest, and Mmhmm.

He had recently posted on Instagram that he would be releasing new music soon and was due to perform at Country Rising festival on Friday.

Organisers posted on their Instagram he would no longer be performing "due to a personal emergency".

Videos on social media showed BigXthaPlug performing at the Iowa State Fair as scheduled on Saturday, where he started his set by saying: "They didn't think I was coming."

He performed at Wireless Festival in the UK in 2025 shortly before releasing his latest album.

In August last year, he was arrested on charges of unlawful possession of a weapon and a small amount of marijuana. The case continues.

He also faced similar charges in 2022.

Entertainment.title: Tupac murder trial: Accused told police in 2008 his nephew fired fatal shots
Entertainment.text:
The man accused of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur told police more than a decade later that he handed the gun used in the drive-by shooting to a passenger who then passed it to his nephew who opened fire on the rapper.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis is on trial in Las Vegas, charged with one count of murder with a deadly weapon over the killing of the rap superstar in 1996. On Thursday jurors heard a recording of a police interview with Davis in 2008.

Prosecutors allege that although Davis did not fire the gun that killed Shakur, he ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further criminal conduct for the gang he helped lead.

Davis, 63, has pleaded not guilty.

His lawyer Michael Sanft has argued that what his client had previously said of his involvement cannot be believed.

Shakur's murder is a cold case that has gripped the public's fascination for 30 years.

Prosecutors allege Davis planned the 7 September 1996 shooting after his nephew Orlando Anderson was involved in a fight with Shakur in Las Vegas hours earlier. They argue that Davis believed the attack on his nephew could not "go unanswered".

Central to the case are testimonies by Davis in the formerly secret 2008 police interview and, later, in a 2019 memoir he co-authored called Compton Street Legend.

Prosecutors on Thursday played the 2008 interview Davis conducted with Los Angeles Police detectives Daryn Dupree and Greg Kading, who were investigating the death of another rapper, Chris Wallace aka The Notorious B.I.G.

Davis described the moment the Cadillac he was a passenger in stopped alongside the car Shakur was in.

"Yeah, if we would've been on my side, I would've blasted," Davis said, according to a transcript.

According to the transcript, Davis said in the interview he passed his gun back to Deandre "Big Dre" Smith, but Smith did not want the weapon.

Anderson, who was also in the back seat, took the weapon and started firing, Davis said.

Anderson died a decade before the interview, having denied any involvement in Shakur's murder.

One of the detectives, Kading, told Davis in reference to a deal for his information: "Nothing you say today can be used against you."

But prosecutors say any agreement was negated when Davis went public with his version in his memoir several years later.

The prosecutor said the book shows Davis was "mad" after his nephew was involved in a fight with Shakur in a Las Vegas casino, with Davis writing: "Them jumping on my nephew gave us the ultimate green light to do something to their ass."

In the memoir he claimed he was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot, and "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat.

Davis has since distanced himself from the book, saying he did not write all of it and that parts were fictionalised to sell more copies.

In the interview played to court, Davis said he repeatedly spoke with Sean "Diddy" Combs and discussed killing Shakur.

The detectives questioned Davis about meetings with Combs during Bad Boy Records tour stops in San Diego, Anaheim, Irvine and Las Vegas.

"Which of those four is it when you talk to him about murdering Tupac?" Kading asked, according to a transcript shown in court, as reported by Reuters.

"It was really about both of them, yeah, either one of them," Davis responded.

"Tupac and Suge?" Kading asked, referring to Death Row Records founder Marion "Suge" Knight, who was with Shakur in the vehicle during the shooting.

"Yeah," Davis responded.

Representatives for Combs did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

However, Davis' lawyer Sanft asked jurors earlier in the trial: "What facts do you have to support any of what Keffe D said in any of his interviews or the book?"

"You have to ask yourself the question: If I just say things, is that going to end up being one of those things where I'm going to be handed up for a murder by just repeating that fiction? I keep repeating that? The answer is no. You have to corroborate everything I say in order for it to be true. Otherwise, it's just that."

Sanft has also said prosecution witnesses were unreliable and the police investigation was riddled with issues.

A former Las Vegas homicide detective told the jury earlier this week that no witnesses had been able to identify the shooter.

Later, a former member of Shakur's entourage, James "Mob James" McDonald, gave evidence that even though he was not there to witness the shooting, those who were there that night within Shakur's circle had quickly communicated who was responsible.

"It was a gang war. People were getting hurt. People were being sought," he said. "Orlando (Anderson), him and certain other people were being sought because people wanted to kill them."

Entertainment.title: ‘I didn’t miss a thing’: How Nick Haymes photographed his sons’ entire lives from verrucas to homemade hamster coffin
Entertainment.text:
Not many family photo albums open with images of the twin towers on fire. But for Nick Haymes, it made perfect sense. “When 9/11 happened,” he says, “I realised life was very short.” At the time, he was living in New York, trying to forge a career, while his friend, colleague and future wife Lina was dealing with the fallout of her previous marriage. “It made us realise we should probably get together and have a family. It was this huge historical event, but on a very micro level, it also shaped my relationship with my wife and children.”

Chronograph is a photography book that runs from those terrorist attacks to the present day, tracing the journey of Haymes’s two sons, Philipp and Lawrence, as they grow from drooling babies into young men. We are given a ringside seat as arms get broken, beloved pets die and hairs start sprouting from armpits. The mundane side of life – verrucas, messy kitchens, Lina cleaning out an ear with a cotton bud – is captured in the same way as birthday parties and rites of passage.

“Because we lived in this tiny, 800 sq ft apartment in Manhattan, you don’t miss a thing, all the ups and downs, all the mood swings,” says Haymes. “There was no door slamming, because there was nowhere to go!”

Indeed, we are not spared from seeing the children at their least flattering: “We used to have a running joke where Lawrence would say: ‘You’re the only parent that would photograph me when I’m crying rather than deal with the issue straight away,’” admits Haymes, “but I like to think I was attentive. It was a funny balance because the camera was always around, but it seemed to work.”

There are also multiple shots of the boys naked – not just running around the house as young children but as they transition into adulthood too. I suspect most teenagers would not be cool with this, but Haymes insists he had their approval. “They don’t have an issue,” he says. “I’ve been lucky enough to have some very nice photographers in my household at various times, so they’re aware of the creative process.” He shrugs: “There are bigger themes in the book than child nudity. That was just a part of our daily life.”

Besides, when Philipp and Lawrence reach their teens – all bleached hair, tattoos and stubble – they work out an ingenious method of rebellion. Instead of sulking or turning away from the camera, Haymes says his kids smiled and put their thumbs up, knowing that the last thing their dad wanted was a posed family portrait. “That was basically their way of telling me to clear out of their lives,” he says.

Born in Stratford-upon-Avon, Haymes hoped to study art but ended up dropping out. “I took way too many drugs in my 20s and had a bit of a breakdown,” he says. After couch-surfing in London for a bit, he found work in a photo studio, eventually assisting Jürgen Teller. In 1999, he packed two cameras into a bag and decided to try his luck in New York. It was here he met Lina, a Jewish refugee who, as a teenager, had moved to the US with her parents from Ukraine – then part of the Soviet Union. She was working on a magazine and gave him a commission that allowed him to get a visa and stay.

Haymes’s own difficult transition from youth to adulthood is perhaps what draws him to his subjects. Between Dog and Wolf captured his road trips across California and Oklahoma with a group of young skateboarders. Follow-up Gabe TM unfurled over many years hanging out with Gabe Nevins, the teenage star of Gus Van Sant’s Paranoid Park. Unexpectedly, Haymes found himself chronicling Nevins’s homelessness and addiction in the wake of making the movie. Dancing on the Fault Line, published in 2024, was another mammoth excursion, following teenager Love Bailey and her extended queer family right up to her decision to transition in her 30s.

Haymes is still in touch with his previous subjects: he shot Bailey’s wedding; Gabe is living a “normal life” now in Oregon; the skaters have children of their own. Haymes doesn’t intend to foster such deep relationships with his subjects. “I always think, ‘Oh, I’ll just do a nice quick shoot.’ But then I get attached to everybody, they become part of my life. You can become a father figure to them, or a therapist maybe. That’s part of it, and that’s part of the educational process for me, just to be with people and understand them.”

It was during Covid that Haymes found the time to go through all his family negatives and work out what to do with them. “It moved me pretty heavily,” he says. “I also had to try to be as impartial as I could because I didn’t want it to be saccharine.”

Did he know, as he took them, that the photos of his children would end up in a published book? “I suppose, as a photographer, yes. But I really did it for personal memory, and as a little self-analysis. To think about how I was as a parent. Also, I shoot on film and at the time, in the early 2000s, digital photography had kicked in so I was finding myself more and more unemployable. I thought, ‘OK, I am becoming a house husband.’ But I wanted to be a photographer still, so the family life around me is what I photographed.”

Besides Lina and the boys, the other key figures in the book are Lina’s parents Nadia and Mikhail. “They were big characters,” says Haymes. “I had to learn how to become a little more emotional and a little more warm and compassionate.”

One striking image is of Mikhail sitting with wrapping paper on his head. He’s in a full tracksuit, giving off a slightly intimidating Paulie Walnuts vibe. “He was a very loving person,” says Haymes, “but yeah, maybe a bit of a rogue. Whereas my mother-in-law had her issues and I think maybe undiagnosed bipolar disorder. She also became a victim of prescription medication in the US, and we had to deal with that. She was certainly a tough mother-in-law, but at some point you fall in love with her anyway.”

There are some portentous images in the book. Scars on Mikhail’s stomach mirror Lina’s caesarean scars, although we can only guess why he’s been cut open. Then there is the pet hamster, who we see being held, adored and then grieved for as it rests in its cardboard coffin.

The book’s closing passages are extremely moving, as we see Nadia and Mikhail in hospital together, their conditions slowly deteriorating. “We were bringing two people to dialysis every day, which was two pretty gruelling years.” At some point, Haymes converted the home art gallery into a hospice.

In the book, it appears as if the couple died at the same time. In reality it was a year apart and the couple had gone through a divorce by that point. “There are things that don’t need to be known,” says Haymes of the story his book tells. “Everybody has a family album, and through those you only remember certain parts.”

Despite their divorce, Nadia and Mikhail were buried together in Los Angeles. “I’m not sure if Lina’s father is enjoying that right now, but that’s what happened,” says Haymes with a smile.

He says he had been asked to make a photography book of his family for 15 years but it was only when the grandparents died that he realised the project was complete. “The book starts with death and ends with death,” he says. “It’s gone full circle.”

Interspersed with beautiful, closeup images of flowers received at the funeral, we see Philipp and Lawrence standing by the graveside with the urn. “For them to be able to communicate those emotions and to speak at a service, for me that felt like, ‘OK, they’re on their own now. They’ve become men.’”

He pauses, then laughs like only a father can. “Having said that,” he adds, “they’re still on my Uber account.”

Entertainment.title: ‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked away
Entertainment.text:
The electronic gates slide open to reveal a gorgeous Portuguese villa, a swimming pool and a beansprout of a man. “You’ve made me feel very important,” says Russ Abbot with a smile. “Come in!”

It’s more than 30 years since Abbot, aged 78, dominated Saturday night TV with his sketches, songs and impersonations. He appealed to all sorts. Kids, parents and grandparents united around the TV – first for Russ Abbot’s Madhouse, which ran from 1980 to 1985, then The Russ Abbot Show, from 1986 to 1991. He was joined by the inimitable Bella Emberg and a cast of young comics, including Les Dennis, Dustin Gee and Michael Barrymore. But make no mistake, it was Abbot’s show and the 80s was his decade. At his peak, he attracted 18 million viewers an episode.

When TV commissioners tired of his brand of sketch comedy, he did stints in the sitcoms Boomers and Last of the Summer Wine and played it straight in the moving TV drama September Song. There was a run of West End musical smashes – Fagin in Oliver!, Roger de Bris in The Producers, Alfred P Doolittle in My Fair Lady. Then, in 2016, he quietly retired. For the past seven years, he has split his time between Barbados and the Algarve, where I find him today.

Abbot introduces me to his wife, Trish, who has a smart silver bob and a northern accent. How long have you two been married, I ask her. “Sixty years,” she says quietly. “Not even the Train Robbers got that!” Trish, 80, giggles.

We’re standing in a large, airy hall. On a table are figurines of Laurel and Hardy – Abbot’s heroes. Upstairs, I can make out lots of framed photos. He takes me on a tour. There are pics of him with the great entertainers of his era (Brucey, Elton, Tarby, Shaky) and the royals (Philip, Anne, Charles). We pass the silver discs from his brief period as Britain’s unlikeliest pop star (who can forget Atmosphere?). “That’s a certificate acknowledging the biggest box office in summer season history,” he says, like an accountant conducting an audit of his success. “And that’s whatshisname.” He squints at a picture. “Live Aid. Bob Geldof.”

Pride of place is a photo of him dressed as Cooperman, with Tommy Cooper. Cooperman was one of Abbot’s more surreal mashup characters – Superman meets the brilliantly bumbling comic giant, who died on stage in 1984. He adored Cooper. “It was so funny at the funeral. All the faces were there. Max Bygraves, Eric Sykes, me. And when the cortege came in, we’d forgotten he’d got a younger brother who looked just like him. He walked in and we’re like: ‘Oh God! Another Tommy prank.’ When the curtain closed on the coffin, I thought: he’s going to come out in a minute because he was such a practical joker.”

He pauses. Now he sounds emotional. “After the funeral, we were walking out paying our respects to his wife, Gwen, and she said to me: ‘He thought you were the cat’s whiskers!’ I filled up. Amazing.”

More photos. Dennis and Gee, the double act who memorably impersonated Coronation Street’s Mavis Riley and Vera Duckworth on his show. Gee died in 1986, at 43. “So talented. Died too young.” We come to a picture of Abbot dressed as CU Jimmy, the incomprehensible, ranting Scottish stereotype that he’d struggle to get away with today. He says the character was based on his Scottish mother, whose accent got thicker the nearer the family got to Scotland for their holidays. He impersonates her – and she sounds as incoherent as Jimmy.

Abbot’s mother, Elizabeth, was in domestic service to the Duke of Westminster at Eaton Hall in Cheshire when she met his father, Don Roberts, a tanker driver for Pratt’s Oil who went on to become an area manager. Young Russell Roberts was a bright lad who went to Chester Grammar. But he became obsessed with drumming, flunked his O-levels and left school at 16 to join a band called the Black Abbots. He supplemented his income with a job as a stagehand at the Royalty theatre in Chester, where the band had a residency.

They soon became a comedy band, with Abbot dismounting the drums to tell daft jokes. The band won the talent show Opportunity Knocks six weeks in a row, became huge in the working men’s clubs, but never had a hit record. By 1973, Abbot was appearing on the TV standup comedy show The Comedians and his manager, Mike Hughes, didn’t think Russell Roberts had a ring to it. He suggested he become Russ Abbot. “He said: ‘Think about it, if your bill is in alphabetical order, you’ll always be top of the bill.’ He said: ‘Abba could top you, but that’s about it.’ That’s clever, isn’t it?”

By the late 1970s, Abbot was well known as a comic and starred in the original Madhouse series with the more famous Freddie Starr. After 17 years as a Black Abbot, he left to go solo. Within months, Russ Abbot’s Madhouse started on ITV (The Russ Abbot Show would move during its run to the BBC) and he was a Saturday night fixture.

We join Trish outside in the shade. She’s made us coffee and piled a plate with digestive biscuits. Did life change when he became a household name? “No.” He looks at her for confirmation. “Just in the sense we moved up the ladder homewise, didn’t we, Trish? So we started in the caravan. Trish’s dad had a win on the pools that paid for the caravan as a wedding present. Then my dad got us a place with £1-a-week rent. Two up, two down. Then we got a £10,000 bungalow and sold it for twice the price.”

“Yep,” says Trish.

‘Then we moved down south, we moved to Wentworth. We looked at this nice house …”

“And that was it, yes,” says Trish.

“We bought it, cash.”

Were loads of women interested in you? “Not really, no,” he says. There’s a glint in his eye. “Oh, I suppose in my drumming days. Early.” The glint vanishes. “Actually, it was more the singers. Because I was just the drummer in the back.” He tells me how he met Trish. “She came to the stage door of the British Legion in Ellesmere Port as I was packing my drums up. We had a bass player in those days called Paul Dodd. He ended up a policeman. Trish says: ‘Is the bass player around?’ I said: ‘No, he’s gone, love.’ She said: ‘Oh, that’s a shame, I wanted to say hello to him.’”

Did you fancy the bass player, I ask Trish.

So you got the wrong bloke?

“Yeah, I got him instead.”

“I said: come on, I’ll buy you a drink. Then I said: let me give you a lift home. She said: I only live across the road. I said: you can’t walk alone at this time of night. So I left with a kiss and a cuddle. And it all started from there, didn’t it, Trish?”

Did she find him funny? “Oh no. Very normal. Lovely brothers, lovely mum and dad. Just normal, like the boy next door.” Did she like comedy? “Oh God, no!” Actually, she says, there was one occasion when he really made her laugh. “He opened the garden fete and chopped his nose off instead of cutting the ribbon.”

Genuinely?

“Yes, he was rushed to hospital. That’s what made me laugh.”

“I had stitches all round my nose.”

Trish is in stitches at the memory.

“But that wasn’t intentionally funny,” Abbot protests.

“No,” says Trish, still hooting. “But it was very funny, Russell. And we’ve laughed ever since.”

He must have been stopped a lot over the years by fans. “No, not really,” he says. “It was always a nod and a wink and a smile. There’s one funny story. We went to the opening show of Miss Saigon.” Trish is already giggling. “We go into the VIP area. We sit there and Trish nudges me. All these heads are turning. And I say: ‘It’s all right! The lights will go down in a minute.’ I say: ‘Trish, it’s a compliment.’ And she nudges me again and says: ‘Look who’s sitting next to me!’ And it was Burt Lancaster. She fell about. Lovely story.”

Abbot never considered himself a star. “I always think I’m playing that role of Russ Abbot. I go in the stage door as Russ Abbot and come out as Russell Roberts.” And he was too reserved to play the big I am. “I never used to like chatshows, because I was shy and I found them embarrassing. It’s like, now I’m retired, I’m not so shy and I can talk about it because it’s past.”

Trish has always been his biggest fan, he says. Then he corrects himself. “Trish and my mum. She used to do handouts for the WI. I’d sign the autograph and she’d sign the back: ‘Russ’s mum!’ She loved it!” In her 70s, his mother got dementia. She went into a home, but Abbot didn’t realise how bad it had got until he arranged for her to come to a show. “Trish brought her up to the dressing room and Mum walked in and said: ‘What a pleasure to meet you. Thank you so much, I’ve been so entertained. It was absolutely marvellous, and now to meet you in person.’

“I stood there and said: ‘Mum, it’s me,’ and she said: ‘I’ll have to go now, my family’s waiting for me.’ So Trish took her back. I slammed the dressing room door three times. It was terrible. It’s a terrible illness. She died about a year later. She was still a very elegant lady, very smartly dressed. She didn’t act like she had dementia. She just couldn’t remember who I was.”

Abbot worked incredibly hard in his heyday. “In 1984, I worked 363 days.” Meanwhile, Trish was working incredibly hard, too, bringing up their four children. “Trish raised them all. I was always away, summer season tour or pantomime. Pantomimes, gosh! You’d get home Christmas Eve, put the presents under the tree, go to bed, have breakfast, watch the kids open the toys and then go back to do a matinee.”

But, he says, they were great times. He tells me of all the wonderful people he worked with. It sounds like an Oscar acceptance speech. Barry Cryer wrote much of his material, but there was a whole team involved and there is not an actor, producer, writer or manager he misses out.

He was the ideas man, he says, rather than the wordsmith. “I loved it. All the nonsense.” He talks about the silly names they invented for characters. “My favourite was Miss Funnyfanny intead of Miss Moneypenny. I think that was my cousin Russell. I loved Basildon Bond because of the silliness of it.”

Suddenly he’s quoting a 40-year-old monologue from a sketch featuring his James Bond parody. ‘My name’s Bond. Basildon Bond, licence to kill and drive a heavy-goods vehicle. I’d been away on holiday when I was summonsed back to headquarters to see my boss P … ‘Was it a good holiday Bond?’ I said: ‘Yes, thank you, sir, I went away for a bit of peace and quiet. I found a nice little piece. I just hope she keeps quiet.’ He said: ‘Don’t bother me with a silly little thing like that.’ I said: ‘It’s funny, that’s what she said.’”

He quotes the monologue word-perfect, in all its anachronistic glory. For all the inappropriateness, there’s also an innocence to it, as there is to him. I notice he doesn’t swear and I ask if he’s religious. “Oh, I believe in God. I say my prayers every night.”

Abbot fell out of fashion in the 1990s, as did virtually all the standup rooted in working men’s clubs and seaside summer seasons. Did he mind when his TV show got cancelled? “I wasn’t distressed or angry or anything. It came about when the head of entertainment gave an interview and said: ‘The BBC’s going to change. No more of this, no more of that,’ and somebody said: ‘Does that mean Russ Abbot?’ and he said yes, meaning the sketch shows. So then it became ‘BBC sacks Russ Abbot’, but that didn’t bother me. I thought: well, I’ve had a very good run. Also, I’d just cracked the West End, so I was doing everything I wanted to do without the stress of the TV shows.”

Why did he fall out of fashion? “It was when the new wave came in. Alternative comedy. I thought, alternative comedy? What’s it alternative to? If the thing’s funny, it’s funny. Political correctness came in, and you can’t laugh at each other and you can’t laugh at yourself. At the same time, a lot of comedy started going blue and I thought: I’m not going down that road.”

So much of his show’s humour was rooted in stereotyping and many of the jokes were at the expense of his great friend Emberg’s weight. Did he understand why that was no longer acceptable? “Yes. Some of the scripts I used to look at myself and wonder. I’d say: ‘Bella, have you read the script?’ and she’d say: ‘Yeah, I think it’s funny’. I’d say: ‘Are you sure?’ and she’d say: ‘Yeah, why?’ ‘I’m just asking your opinion,’ and she’d say: ‘I think it’s hilarious,’ and I’d say: ‘So do I!’” Did she ever get upset? “No, she never got upset once.” Emberg died in 2018 at 80. Of all the people he’s worked with, he says he misses her most.

I loved it when Emberg as Blunderwoman lifted Abbot over her shoulders and carried him off. Even at his heaviest, he weighed only 12 and a half stone. Not much for a man over six foot tall. These days, Emberg would have had even less trouble. He’s lost two and a half stone. He knows Trish is worried, but he’s had every test going and nothing has been diagnosed. As for Trish, he says, she’s had two strokes in the past year, so they are taking it easy. Which doesn’t mean they’re not up to a round of golf. Abbot is a fine player and used to play off a handicap of 12, but he insists Trish is better than him. To be fair, so does she.

Stories circulated that Abbot retired because he was embittered that comedy had changed and no straight roles were being offered to him. It’s true that he’s not a great fan of today’s comedy, he says, and he was disappointed when Boomers and Last of the Summer Wine were cancelled, but he insists the stories are nonsense. He actually retired because Hughes, his manager, was retiring and he thought it was a good time to call it quits and spend more time with Trish and have a social life.

“I’ve seen something on YouTube saying ‘The tragedy of Russ Abbot’ and ‘He’s run away to Portugal’.” He smiles.

“We just watched it once,” says Trish. “I said, don’t watch it, Russell.”

It doesn’t look much of a tragedy to me, I say, glancing out at the cloudless sky, swimming pool and topiaried bushes.

“Thank you,” Trish says.

“I’ve had a wonderful career,” Abbot says. “Wonderful!”

“He’s always said that,” Trish says.

And now you’re enjoying a richly deserved retirement? “Absolutely,” he says.

How would Trish feel if he decided to go back to work? Her eyes light up. “Happy,” she says. Why? “I’d like him to do something like Last of the Summer Wine. I think he does miss it, I’ve got to say.”

Abbot gives her a look. “Yeah!” he says. “But not desperately, Trish.”
